1077-the-mirror-of-kong-ho:
Ernest Bramah invents Kong Ho, a Chinese gentleman who writes home about England with grave courtesy and total misunderstanding. Trains, teapots, policemen, and English manners all pass through his polite, literal gaze, and the result is satire aimed at both East and West. The letters first ran as a series.

Kong Ho's formal English and his Confucian maxims turn London life upside down, and his mishaps grow funnier as he grows bolder. Bramah, famed for his Kai Lung tales, writes here with a lighter, more mocking hand. The book charms readers who enjoy wit that cuts both ways.
1593-how-to-tell-the-birds-from-the-flow:
Robert Williams Wood's Manual of Flornithology for Beginners, published by Paul Elder and Company in 1907, is a book of jokes in verse and picture. Each page pairs a bird with a flower it resembles, from a catbird to a pussywillow, and asks the reader to tell one from the other by rhyme and drawing.

Wood, a physicist with a playful pen, delights in puns and look-alikes, and the illustrations carry half the humour. The book is slight, silly, and charming. It is a period piece of American whimsy, best enjoyed as a gift book for nature lovers with a taste for wordplay.
3268-the-mysteries-of-udolpho:
Ann Radcliffe's great gothic romance runs to three volumes in this edition, with poems interspersed through the prose. Emily St Aubert, orphaned and tender, passes into the power of the villain Montoni and his castle of Udolpho, high in the Apennines. Veiled pictures, midnight music, and locked doors supply the terrors, all in Radcliffe's rich, scenic prose.

The mysteries, famously, admit natural explanations in the end, but the dread they raise is real while it lasts. Radcliffe invented the female gothic here: a heroine whose sensibility is both her danger and her defense. Readers who enjoy castles, villains, and sublime landscape will find the original pattern, imitated ever since and never quite outdone.
5171-thomas-hariot-the-mathematician-the:
Henry Stevens's study gathers what could be known in the nineteenth century about Thomas Hariot, the Elizabethan mathematician, philosopher, and scholar. Hariot's only published works were his Briefe and True Report on Virginia and a posthumous algebra. He also observed comets, corresponded with Kepler, and anticipated the law of refraction.

Stevens prints letters, including Hariot's correspondence with Sir William Lower at Sion. He adds biographical and bibliographical notes on Hariot's associates. The book serves as a record of a brilliant, half-lost scientific life. It remains useful for readers interested in the quiet scholars behind the age of exploration.
6393-the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-vol:
Ferentum in Etruria gives Otho his ancestors, an ancient and honourable family among the most considerable of the region. His grandfather, son of a Roman knight and a mother of uncertain birth, was educated in Livia Augusta's house and rose to praetor but no higher. His father Lucius, nobly descended on his mother's side and dearly beloved by Tiberius, so resembled the emperor in features that most people believed a closer tie.

A. Salvius Otho's own rise turns on omens, the advice of Seleucus, and a signal word from a freedman about architects come, agreed beforehand. Waiting accomplices stand in the Forum by Saturn's temple at the gilded milestone, while Otho pays respects to Galba, hears the augur, and moves. Suetonius writes a short reign begun in conspiracy, where birth, favour, and timing decide an empire in a morning.
6918-the-history-of-the-reign-of-ferdina:
William Prescott tells the reign of Ferdinand and Isabella the Catholic in three volumes, and this is the first. He dedicates the work to his father, William Prescott, guide of his youth and best friend in riper years, with warm filial affection. His preface notes that English writers had covered Spanish reigns from Charles the Fifth onward, yet no full account of this earlier turning point existed.

Prescott therefore takes up the Catholic monarchs whose rule joined Spain and opened a new age for Europe. The volume opens the story with the state of the peninsula and the forces that shaped the reign. Later volumes carry the tale forward, but this first book lays the ground for a history long praised for learning and for narrative power.
6967-the-history-of-the-reign-of-ferdina:
Prescott's second volume on Ferdinand and Isabella continues the reign with the internal affairs of the kingdom and the war in Granada. Chapter twelve treats the Inquisition in Aragon, Isabella enforcing the laws, the marriage of Catharine of Navarre, the freeing of Catalan serfs, and the remonstrances of the Cortes. A conspiracy and the murder of Arbues lead to cruel persecutions across Ferdinand's dominions.

Chapter thirteen turns to war, with the surrender of Velez Malaga, the siege and conquest of Malaga, and the narrow escape of Ferdinand himself. The queen visits the camp, the town is summoned, and civil feuds among the Moors shape the fight. Only this second volume's matter is described here, in Prescott's learned and vivid narrative.
6968-the-history-of-the-reign-of-ferdina:
Prescott's third volume on Ferdinand and Isabella turns to the Italian wars and the partition of Naples. Chapter ten follows Louis the Twelfth's designs on Italy, the French conquest of Milan, alarm at the Spanish court, and bold remonstrance to the Pope. Gonsalvo de Cordova sails with a fleet, the partition of Naples is confirmed by the Pope, and Italy stands astonished at French success and cruelty.

Gonsalvo then overruns Calabria, invests Tarento, punishes a mutiny, and presses a bolder plan of attack, despite discontents in his army. Only this third volume's matter is described here, from the Italian campaigns onward. Prescott writes with the same command of sources and narrative pace that mark the whole history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ayacucho: Ayacucho, also called Guamanga, is a Peruvian diocese under Lima. Paul V erected the See of Guamanga on 20 July 1609. It stood vacant from 1821 to 1838, when it was transferred to Ayacucho. The diocese counts 200,610 Catholics, with 96 parishes, 120 secular priests, and 212 churches or chapels. No further history, bishop, or event is given beyond those dates and figures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-c:
This reference entry examines the councils of Clovesho, a place in the Anglo-Saxon Church whose exact site has never been pinned down. It weighs rival guesses, from Abingdon to Tewkesbury and Cliff-at-Hoo. Each guess, it concludes, rests on shaky ground, while the councils themselves and their acts are genuine.

The story starts with Archbishop Theodore's 673 decree that yearly synods meet at Clofeshoch. From there it follows the recorded councils through the eighth century, including debates over church privilege and discipline. The entry leans on Bede, Haddan and Stubbs, and other standard collections. It makes a useful guide to an early English church puzzle that still resists a tidy answer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giacomo-rho:
Giacomo Rho was a Jesuit missionary born at Milan in 1593, who died at Peking in 1638. Son of a noble jurist, he entered the Society of Jesus at twenty and, after weak early studies, grew strong in mathematics. Ordained at Rome by Cardinal Bellarmine, he sailed for the Far East in 1617 with forty-four companions. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces his path from Macao to the imperial court.

At Macao, during a Dutch siege, he taught the people to use artillery, and that service opened China to him. He quickly learned the language, and in 1631 the emperor called him to Peking to reform the Chinese calendar. With Father Schall he worked at that hard task until his death. Many Chinese officials attended his funeral, and he left writings on the calendar, astronomy, and theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-idaho:
Idaho, probably from an Arapaho word meaning Gem of the Mountains, was first suggested as a name for Colorado territory. A Pacific Slope state shaped roughly like a rudder, it stretches nearly five hundred miles south from Canada. It is bounded by Utah and Nevada, Oregon and Washington, Wyoming and Montana, and British Columbia. Its area exceeds eighty-three thousand square miles, a third of it government forest reserves.

Central Idaho is vast and mountainous, holding the Salmon River, Lost River, Sawtooth, Boise, Seven Devils, and other well-timbered ranges. Its mean elevation nears forty-seven hundred feet, with extremes from under eight hundred to over twelve thousand feet. The Bitter Root range, part of the Continental Divide, forms much of the eastern border, and the entry goes on to the state's climate, resources, people, and church history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jericho:
Jericho, the City of Palm Trees, appears here as three successive towns on neighbouring sites. The first, Canaanite Jericho, fell to Joshua after the Jordan crossing, later housed Benjamin's town, suffered under Moab's Eglon, sheltered David's envoys. It was rebuilt under Ahab by Hiel of Bethel.

Elisha purified its spring, exiles repopulated it after captivity, and Bacchides fortified it for Syria. Digs in 1907 and 1908 at Tell es-Sultan uncovered an 840-yard rampart, a double-walled citadel, kings' houses, and later Jewish pottery. The entry then follows Jericho's later towns down to the modern village near the spring.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-labarum-chi-r:
The labarum was the military standard Constantine the Great adopted after his vision of a cross of light. Eusebius pictures it as a long gold-covered spear with a crossbar, crowned by a wreath of gold and jewels holding the Chi-Rho, the interlaced first letters of Christ's name.

From the crossbar hung a square purple banner, rich with gems and gold, inscribed in Greek Touto nika, conquer by this sign, rendered in Latin as In hoc signo vinces. Medallions of the emperor and his children adorned the staff, and fifty picked guardsmen defended the standard. Similar standards went to all legions, the monogram was cut on shields, and coins show its changing forms, though the symbol itself predated Constantine's conversion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marcus-salviu:
Marcus Salvius Otho was Roman emperor after Galba and Nero, born at Rome on 28 April 32 and dead at Brixellum on the Po on 15 April 69. At Nero's court he lived loosely, and as husband of Poppaea Sabina he was posted to Lusitania as governor, for form's sake.

When Galba was proclaimed emperor, Otho returned with him to Rome. Against Galba's miserliness, Otho courted troops with gifts. On 15 January 69, five days after Galba named Piso his heir, twenty-three soldiers proclaimed Otho emperor in the street. Galba was murdered at the Forum, and the senate confirmed Otho. Vitellius, proclaimed at Cologne, marched from Germany with a third of the army behind him. Otho restored Nero's statues, recalled Nero's exiles, and put Tigellinus to death. He marched north on 14 March, lost near Cremona on 14 April before eastern legions joined him, and killed himself the next day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-agath:
Agatho was born in Sicily toward the end of the sixth century. He is believed to have lived as a Benedictine monk at Palermo's St Hermes. He was over one hundred when he took the papal chair in 678 as successor to Donus. Soon after, Wilfred of York came to Rome after Theodore of Canterbury deposed him unjustly. At a Lateran synod Agatho restored Wilfred to his see.

The chief event of his reign was the Sixth Ecumenical Council at Constantinople in 680. Papal legates presided, and the council practically ended the Monothelite heresy. Agatho died before its decrees reached Rome for his approval. He was buried in St Peter's on 10 January 681. He was famed for affability and charity, and for many miracles he is called Thaumaturgus, the Wonderworker.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zakho:
Zakho is a Chaldean diocese matching the ancient see of Maalta, once suffragan of Adiabene or Arbela. Nestorian bishops appear there from the fifth to the seventh century in Chabot's Synodicon Orientale. The see stayed joined to Akra and Amadia until the mid-nineteenth century, when the province split into three dioceses: Amadia, Zakho, and Akra-Zehbar, with Zakho dating from 1859. Today Zakho province belongs to the Mossul vilayet, and its city holds 2500 people, 1500 Jews and 100 Christians, on an island in the Little Khabour.

The diocese counts 3500 Catholics, ten resident priests, five religious of Saint Hormisdas's congregation, fifteen parishes or stations, twenty churches and chapels, and one primary school. Its small Catholic flock lives among a largely Jewish town population on the upper Tigris frontier.
doe-osti-17076220-development-of-an-ultr: Sound speed in molten salts got measured, and this DOE report covers the ultrasonic pulse-echo system development. The pages detail the instrument. The reactor chemists get their ears. The salts were molten. The instrument was ultrasonic. The chemists got ears.
doe-osti-3002044-diversion-path-analysis: Sneaky fuel theft at salt reactors got its DOE playbook, and this text maps how thieves might try it. The pages detail the guard plan. The safeguards crew gets its framework. The reactors were molten salt. The plan was guard.
doe-osti-3013661-studying-f-electron-con: Thorium molecules got f-electroned, and this DOE text studies uranium compounds. The pages detail the contribution findings. The chemists get their data. The electrons were f. The data were chemist. The molecules were thorium. The uranium was containing. The contributions were f-electron.
doe-osti-3022912-ultra-wide-bandgap-lase: Photoconductors got laser-addressed, and this DOE text covers ultra-wide bandgaps. The pages detail the findings. The materials folks get their data. The bandgap was ultra wide. The data were material. The addressable were laser. The photoconductors were bandgap.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DouglasMikeShow: A letter dated December 2, 1967 was written to Shelley Andrews of The Mike Douglas Show, the popular television talk program. The writer discusses a book about Lee Harvey Oswald that was about to be published, along with a related speaking trip. The author's name cannot be recovered from the garbled text, so the letter survives as an unsigned piece of a book publicity effort.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIRoweGaryThom: Warren Brown wrote a piece called The Strange Life of an FBI Informer about Gary Thomas Rowe, a man who informed for the Bureau. Rowe's double life, paid source inside violent circles, made his story worth a feature. The surviving record gives the author, title, and subject but no date or detail, so the article stands as a named profile of one informer's career.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HooversNotesKin: Martin Waldron reported for The New York Times that several books were planned on the Ray case, with the first due out the next week. James Earl Ray stood accused of killing Martin Luther King Jr., and publishers moved fast to tell his story. The surviving record gives the author, paper, and headline but no date in the evidence, so the piece stands as Times coverage of the coming Ray books.
how-to-tell-the-birds-from-the-flowers-a:
Robert Williams Wood, a Johns Hopkins physicist, wrote and illustrated How to Tell the Birds from the Flowers in 1907 as a manual of flornithology for beginners. Each page pairs a bird with a similar-sounding plant: the clover and the plover, the crow and the crocus, the parrot and the carrot, the hen and the lichen. Short verses explain the difference, badly on purpose.

The tern and turnip pair shows the method: cooked to a turn, the turnip may be inferred changed to the bird, while the tern is glad he is not in the pot. Wood's nonsense became a small classic of scientific humor, reprinted for a century and loved by naturalists with a weakness for puns.
podcast-dannyjones-FTCiHvay0ho:
Dan Thayer talks with Danny Jones about a hard childhood and a death row case. The episode title frames Thayer as an inmate explaining his early years. Their sample opens far from prison, with hurricane cleanup in Naples.

Thayer describes rich and poor areas hit by the same storm. From there the talk turns back to his youth and choices. Jones asks how early harm shaped later violence. The episode aims for an origin story, told plainly, for listeners who want to understand a condemned man's path rather than just his crime.
podcast-dannyjones-xEmVrE-qSho:
Matt LaCroix returns to Danny Jones with a newly found ancient text that he warns could destroy the church. The episode title quotes that warning. LaCroix studies old texts and lost history, and he treats this find as a bomb.

LaCroix lays out what the text says, where it was found, and who kept it hid, as he tells it. He argues its words clash with the church's core tale. Jones asks how scholars can test the find. Listeners get a bold claim made in full by its top voice. The library files the talk as an archive record, without a verdict.
podcast-joerogan-0H5LCLljJho:
Author Graham Hancock and geologist Randall Carlson join Joe Rogan for episode 872 of the Joe Rogan Experience. The pair are famed as a team for the claim that comet hits felled a high Ice Age culture. Carlson is a field man of rocks and floods.

Hancock and Carlson lay out the signs they read in stone and soil for a vast cataclysm. They argue the blow reset the human tale and left myths as its trace. Rogan gives the pair his long form to teach. Listeners get the core talk that built their fame. The library keeps the episode as a record of their stated case.
podcast-joerogan-ASYtDNoaeHo:
Author Lawrence Wright joins Joe Rogan to tell what he learned of Jim Jones by talking with the cult leader's sons. Wright is a Pulitzer-winning writer on faith and cults. Jones led the Peoples Temple to mass death in Guyana.

Wright tells how the sons' tales reshaped his grasp of their father and his hold on his flock. He shares what life was like for boys raised in the cult's core. Rogan asks how a man so mad drew so many. Listeners get a deep, sad tale told by a top hand. The library holds the segment as an archive record. Note: the older summary says Wright talked with Jones's followers; the title says his sons.
podcast-joerogan-FqMsJZ2SRHo:
Duncan Trussell marks a milestone with episode 2000 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Trussell, the comedian-philosopher who has appeared on the show more than almost anyone, was the natural pick for the landmark number. The visit feels like a reunion as much as an interview.

The two range over their usual shared ground: psychedelics, death, love, and the comedy inside all of it. Rogan looks back at how far the show has come since Trussell's early visits. For fans, the episode is a celebration entry, proof of how much of the show's heart lives in this one friendship.
podcast-joerogan-K9qF687OZho:
What former intelligence official Christopher Mellon thinks of Bob Lazar is the question in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Mellon, who served at the top of U.S. intelligence, helped bring military UFO videos to the public. Lazar is the famous Area 51 claimant. Their names rarely meet.

Rogan works through Mellon's measured public statements and what they imply about Lazar's decades-old story. The talk weighs insider caution against outsider certainty, and asks why officials speak so carefully on this subject. The segment is a short, sharp study in how disclosure figures judge each other's claims.
podcast-joerogan-NY3Zg37nIHo:
Magician David Blaine joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1527. Blaine is famous less for tricks than for endurance feats: buried, frozen, and starved in public view. Rogan, a fan of people who test limits, gives him a long and admiring hearing.

Blaine explains how he trains his body and mind to hold breath, bear cold, and stay calm when panic would kill him. Rogan asks what the feats cost him and why he keeps raising the stakes. The episode is a study in discipline disguised as a chat about magic, full of stories no stage show could hold.
podcast-joerogan-rz0g7kptNHo:
Episode 2078 of the Joe Rogan Experience is Duncan Trussell's later-era return, and the chemistry is unchanged. Trussell, by then a veteran guest, slips straight back into his cosmic comic mode. Rogan gives him the long leash his fans expect.

The talk wanders through troubled times with jokes about death, love, and the end of the world. Trussell finds warmth in dark subjects and turns fear into play. Rogan laughs hard and shares his own takes on aging and fame. It is comfort listening for fans: the Trussell charm, undimmed after hundreds of episodes.
podcast-tuckercarlson-8SwvBVKwBHo:
Former Senate aide Tara Reade tells Tucker Carlson how her life moved to Russia. Reade had accused Joe Biden of assault from his Senate years. Biden denied the claim, and her story drew hard scrutiny.

Reade says she feared arrest or worse if she stayed in America. She describes exile as the price of speaking out. Carlson presents her as a woman punished for an accusation. Listeners hear her full account in her own words. The episode suits those who want the claim heard whole, with its doubts left for them to weigh.
podcast-tuckercarlson-p7ZGf_QEyho:
Tucker Carlson reports on Gaza in a grave episode that calls the war there the holocaust of our time. The title also says Israel shut down the holiest site in Christendom. Carlson speaks in his own voice with a clear charge.

Carlson lays out the death toll as he reads it and the pain of Christians caught in the war. He argues the West looks away while a holy land is crushed. He names the leaders he blames for the silence. Listeners get his full case in one place. The library keeps the episode as a record of his stated view.
ramuntcho:
Ramuntcho, by Pierre Loti, in Henri Pene du Bois's English translation, opens on an autumn evening in the Pyrenean country near Spain. Sad curlews, heralds of autumn, flee in a gray squall. They cross the cold mouths of the Adour, the Nivelle, and the Bidassoa. Their cries ring the half-death of the year.

Ramuntcho walks alone on a moss-covered path in rope soles. Supple and silent, he climbs from far away. His goal is his isolated house in deep shade near the Spanish frontier. Around him the corn stands dead straw in the valleys, beeches and oaks shed their leaves, and the wet earth gives off an odorous damp.
rung-ho:
Talbot Mundy's Rung Ho, headed as a novel from 1914, is shown here at Chapter IX. It stands under a short verse asking God to speed the speaker's master and give him a lead in the line. Dawn is barely breaking at a little mission house. A flea-bitten gray pony is saddled by a sleepy groom and brought round from an open-sided thatch stable in the rear. The violet and mauve before the harsh yellow glare fade as a coppersmith bird starts its endless bong-bong-bong and monkeys chatter in a near baobab tree.

On the stroke of sunrise Rosemary McClean steps out, settles her sun-helmet, and mounts with no help. Dark rings beneath dark eyes show the work of heat and sleepless worry on a girl of twenty. The narrator says she should have graced the cool, rain-swept hills of Scotland.
the-excellence-of-the-rosary-conferences:
Rev. M. J. Frings's The Excellence of the Rosary gives conferences for devotions in honour of the Blessed Virgin, printed at New York with a 1912 copyright. Church approvals head the book: a censor's nihil obstat and the imprimatur of John Cardinal Farley, dated September 19, 1912. Contents move from the devotion's name and origin to its power, then walk through each prayer.

Sign of the cross, creed, Our Father, Hail Mary, and Glory Be each get a talk. Later heads weigh the rosary's form and its mysteries. Frings wrote for sodalities of the Virgin.
the-history-of-the-reign-of-ferdinand-an: William H. Prescott wrote History of the Reign of Ferdinand and Isabella, the Catholic, in three volumes, and the pages present are marked Vol. III. The contents of Volume III outline Part Second, chapter ten, on the Italian wars and the partition of Naples, following Gonsalvo de Cordova through Calabria, the storming of St. George, and the surrender of Tarento, then chapter eleven on the rupture with France. Only the title page and contents outline are present here.
the-history-of-university-education-in-m: Bernard C. Steiner, A.M., fellow in history, wrote The History of University Education in Maryland, in the Johns Hopkins University Studies in Historical and Political Science, ninth series, printed at Baltimore in March-April 1891. The same issue carries The Johns Hopkins University (1876-1891) by Daniel C. Gilman, president of the university. The contents list colonial attempts to found a college, the first and second University of Maryland, Cokesbury College, and other extinct colleges. Only the title page and contents are present here.
the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-volume-0:
Volume eight of Suetonius's Lives of the Twelve Caesars, in Alexander Thomson's translation revised by T. Forester, gives the life of Aulus Salvius Otho. His ancestors came from Ferentum and ranked among the most considerable families in Etruria. His grandfather, raised in Livia Augusta's household, became a senator through her favor but rose no higher than praetor.

His father Lucius Otho was so dearly loved by Tiberius, and resembled him so closely, that many believed Tiberius was his father. Lucius governed with strict severity, even executing soldiers under his own eyes for killing their generals during a revolt against Claudius. Suetonius sketches a family of favor and harsh discipline behind the short-lived emperor.
the-mirror-of-kong-ho:
Ernest Bramah's The Mirror of Kong Ho presents letters from Kong Ho, a Chinese gentleman living among the Westerners of London. A publisher's note calls the letters lively and amusing, written home to China. Kong Ho calls his hosts barbarians and finds endless food for thought in their aids to life, such as the motor car and the piano, both unknown in China at the time. His introduction addresses the 'estimable barbarian' who suggested printing the letters.

Kong Ho promises undeviating fidelity to what he directly observed, though he admits he may have misunderstood an involved allusion. He contrasts his care with travelers who loot Chinese palaces and then publish subtly imagined calumnies. Impartiality, he insists, sways his brush, and truth lurks within his inkpot. He asks that his host's own remarks be left unchanged, as a test and proof to readers.
the-mysteries-of-udolpho:
Ann Radcliffe's romance The Mysteries of Udolpho, interspersed with pieces of poetry as its title announces, is present here only in a contents list, so the Gothic tale itself does not appear. The list divides the novel into volumes, each with its own numbered chapters. Volume I runs to thirteen chapters and Volume II to twelve.

Volume III's list is cut short at Chapter VII in the pages shown, and a fourth volume is not reached. Nothing here names Emily, Montoni, or the castle of Udolpho, and no line of Radcliffe's prose is included. Only the scale of the work, four volumes of short numbered chapters, can be judged from this frame.
the-rover-boys-on-the-river-or-the-searc:
Ninth in its series, The Rover Boys on the River is subtitled The Search for the Missing Houseboat. Arthur Winfield's introduction greets that number with some wonder. Nine volumes struck him as a great many tales about one set of boys. The story itself is complete.

The contents follow the boys through plans for an outing. They say good-bye to Putnam Hall. Days at home follow before they board a houseboat. Flapp and Baxter plot mischief along the way. A queer captain adds to the trouble. Then the houseboat itself disappears. Later headings promise horse thieves and a search on the river. A rescue closes the book.
thomas-hariot-the-mathematician-the-phil:
Henry Stevens of Vermont built his life of Thomas Hariot chiefly from dormant materials, with notices of Hariot's associates. A modern note adds that Hariot worked out the law of refraction early, wrote to Kepler, and watched comets. His only printed works were a Virginia report and a posthumous algebra handbook.

Stevens calls Hariot the first historian of Virginia and traces the land from Ponce de Leon's Terra Florida onward. French planting, Spanish destruction, and Raleigh's English foothold all enter his research. Readers get biography mixed with bibliography and the early history of English Virginia.
